stem: Your support agent has two tools with nearly identical descriptions: `analyze_content` ("Analyze content and return insights") and `analyze_document` ("Analyze a document and return insights"). The model routes requests to the wrong one roughly half the time. What is the single most effective fix?

options.A: Rewrite the two descriptions so each states its distinct purpose, inputs, and outputs
options.B: Delete one of the tools and route every analysis request through the survivor
options.C: Lower the model temperature to 0 so tool selection becomes deterministic and repeatable
options.D: Force `tool_choice: any` so the model is required to pick one of the two on every turn

explanation: Tool descriptions are the PRIMARY mechanism the model uses to select tools, so overlapping, vague descriptions cause misrouting. Differentiating each description — purpose, inputs, outputs, and when to use it versus the other — and ideally renaming to remove the overlap (e.g. `analyze_web_page`) is what restores selection accuracy. Nothing else in (B), (C) or (D) touches the semantics the model actually reads.

distractors.B: Deleting a tool discards a genuinely needed capability to work around a wording problem; the defect is description overlap, not tool count.
distractors.C: Temperature changes sampling randomness, not semantics — at any temperature the model still cannot tell two interchangeable descriptions apart.
distractors.D: `tool_choice: any` forces some call to happen but gives the model no extra information about which of the two ambiguous tools is correct.

stem: Your MCP server exposes the company return policy, product SKU catalog, and shipping-zone reference tables so the agent can reason from them. It also exposes the ability to issue a refund. Which mapping to MCP primitives is correct?

options.A: Expose the policy, catalog, and shipping tables as resources, and refund issuance as a tool
options.B: Expose all four as tools, since every one of them is backed by the same internal service
options.C: Expose all four as resources, since the agent only ever reads data from the backend
options.D: Expose the policy and catalog as tools, and expose refund issuance as a read-only resource

explanation: Resources are application-controlled, read-only reference data the model reasons FROM (catalogs, policies, schemas). Tools are model-controlled ACTIONS with side effects. Issuing a refund moves money, so it must be a tool; the three reference tables are static read-only data, so they belong as resources. (A) is the only split that puts each item on the right side of that line.

distractors.B: Modeling static reference data as tools forces exploratory tool calls to read data the agent could have simply been given, and misuses the action primitive.
distractors.C: Issuing a refund has side effects, so it cannot be a resource; resources are read-only data the host supplies, not actions the model triggers.
distractors.D: This reverses the control model on both sides at once: read-only data becomes model-invoked actions and a money-moving action becomes read-only data.

stem: An MCP tool definition omits the `annotations` block entirely. Given the MCP spec's default annotation values, how will a host most reasonably treat this tool?

options.A: As invalid, because the `annotations` block is required on every tool definition
options.B: As read-only and idempotent, because omitting annotations signals a safe, side-effect-free tool
options.C: As identical to a tool that sets all four annotation hints explicitly to false
options.D: As potentially destructive and open-world, because both of those hints default to true

explanation: The default annotation values assume the worst case: `destructiveHint` defaults to true and `openWorldHint` defaults to true, while `readOnlyHint` and `idempotentHint` default to false. An un-annotated tool is therefore treated as potentially destructive and interacting with external entities — dangerous until proven safe — which is what (D) describes.

distractors.A: Annotations are optional hints, not required fields; a tool definition without them is well-formed and hosts must still be able to call it.
distractors.B: This inverts the defaults. `readOnlyHint` and `idempotentHint` both default to false, so omission signals the opposite of safety.
distractors.C: All-false differs from the defaults in two places: `destructiveHint` and `openWorldHint` default to true, so explicit falses would make the tool look safer than the defaults do.

stem: Your team wants a Slack MCP server and a PostgreSQL MCP server available to everyone who clones the repo, with credentials supplied per-developer via environment variables and never committed. Where should this configuration live?

options.A: In the project's `CLAUDE.md`, so the server setup instructions travel with the repo on clone
options.B: In each developer's user-scoped `~/.claude.json`, configured once by hand on every machine
options.C: In a project-scoped `.mcp.json` committed to the repo, using `${VAR}` for credentials
options.D: In a `.mcp.json` with credentials hardcoded, added to `.gitignore` so it is never pushed

explanation: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` is git-tracked, so it reaches everyone who clones the repo, and `${VAR}` expansion keeps secrets out of the committed file while letting each developer supply their own credentials from the environment. (C) is the only option that satisfies both halves of the requirement — shared config and uncommitted secrets.

distractors.A: CLAUDE.md carries instructions the model reads, not server configuration the client loads; MCP servers declared there are never started.
distractors.B: User scope is per-machine and invisible to a clone, so every developer would have to configure both servers manually and nothing travels with the repo.
distractors.D: Gitignoring the file defeats the goal of sharing it, and hardcoding credentials means the file cannot be committed even if you wanted to.

stem: In `.mcp.json`, a server URL is written as `"url": "${API_BASE_URL}/mcp"`. A developer who has not set `API_BASE_URL` in their environment tries to start Claude Code. What happens, and what one-character-class change would make it resilient?

options.A: It silently substitutes an empty string, so the server simply fails to connect; no change is needed
options.B: Startup fails because the variable is unset; `${API_BASE_URL:-https://acme.io}` supplies a fallback default
options.C: It prompts the developer interactively for the value; switch to `${?API_BASE_URL}` to suppress the prompt
options.D: It falls back to localhost automatically; add `${API_BASE_URL!localhost}` to override that fallback

explanation: `${VAR}` expands to the variable's value and FAILS when the variable is unset — startup errors rather than degrading silently. The `${VAR:-default}` form substitutes the supplied default when the variable is unset, which is the one-character-class change (`:-`) that makes the config resilient, as (B) states.

distractors.A: `${VAR}` does not silently become empty; expansion fails outright, so the failure is loud and the config needs a real fix.
distractors.C: There is no `${?VAR}` interactive-prompt syntax in `.mcp.json` expansion; the supported forms are `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}`.
distractors.D: There is no automatic localhost fallback and no `${VAR!default}` syntax; inventing one leaves the unset variable failing exactly as before.

stem: A customer asks the agent to refund $750. Company policy caps agent-initiated refunds at $500; anything higher must go through a manager workflow. The `process_refund` MCP tool detects the violation. How should it report this so the agent behaves correctly?

options.A: Return a JSON-RPC protocol error with code -32603 so the client framework handles the failure
options.B: Return `isError: true` with `isRetryable: false` and a message pointing to the manager workflow
options.C: Return `isError: true` with `errorCategory: "transient"` and `isRetryable: true` so the agent retries
options.D: Return an empty success result so the agent moves on to the next step without refunding

explanation: A policy cap is a business-rule violation: retrying the same $750 request will always fail, and the model needs to see the failure so it can offer the customer the manager-approval path instead. That means `isError: true` in the result (visible to the model), `isRetryable: false`, and a customer-friendly explanation naming the alternative — which is (B).

distractors.A: Protocol errors go in the JSON-RPC `error` field, which the model never sees, so the agent cannot explain the cap or route the customer to manager approval.
distractors.C: Marking a permanent business rule as transient and retryable sends the agent into retries of a request that can never succeed at $750.
distractors.D: An empty success result hides the violation; the agent has no signal that anything failed and may tell the customer the refund went through.

stem: An MCP client sends a request naming a tool that the server does not expose (a typo in the tool name). At which layer of MCP's two-layer error model does this surface, and can the model reason about it?

options.A: As a JSON-RPC protocol error in the `error` field; the model generally does not see it
options.B: As a silently dropped message; neither the client nor the model receives any error at all
options.C: As both a protocol error and an `isError: true` result, so the model sees the failure twice
options.D: As a tool execution error (`isError: true` in the result); the model sees it and can recover

explanation: Unknown tool names, invalid arguments, and server-level failures are protocol errors and go in the JSON-RPC `error` field (e.g. code -32602). The model does NOT see protocol errors, as (A) says. Only tool-execution errors returned in the `result` with `isError: true` are visible to the model for recovery reasoning.

distractors.B: The protocol returns a structured JSON-RPC error response; the request is rejected explicitly, not dropped without a trace.
distractors.C: An unknown tool is rejected at the protocol layer before any handler runs, so there is no execution result to carry an `isError` flag.
distractors.D: `isError` reports the execution-time failure of a valid tool call; a name the server does not expose never reaches execution.

stem: A document-analysis subagent's `fetch_source` tool hits a 30-second network timeout. The subagent returns `{"status": "error", "message": "failed"}` to the coordinator, which immediately re-issues the identical request and times out again. What is the core problem with this error reporting?

options.A: The error should have been a protocol error so the coordinator's framework retries it automatically
options.B: The subagent should have returned an empty success result rather than alarming the coordinator
options.C: The error carries no structured context — failure type, what was attempted, or any alternatives
options.D: The coordinator should never retry a subagent; every subagent failure must escalate to a human

explanation: A generic `"failed"` status hides everything the coordinator needs in order to recover well: the failure type (a transient timeout), what was attempted, any partial results, and possible alternative sources. With that structured context — the gap (C) names — the coordinator could back off, try an alternate source, or proceed with partial data instead of blindly re-issuing the identical request.

distractors.A: Protocol errors are hidden from the model, so this would remove what little signal the coordinator has, and blind framework retry repeats the same timeout without new information.
distractors.B: Reporting a failure as an empty success suppresses the error entirely; the coordinator would treat missing data as a complete answer.
distractors.D: Retrying a transient timeout is legitimate and usually cheap; the defect is the missing context that would tell the coordinator whether a retry is worth it.

stem: A `search_orders` tool returns `{"results": []}` in two different situations: (1) the orders database was unreachable, and (2) the query ran successfully but the customer genuinely has no matching orders. The agent treats both the same and tells the customer "you have no orders." What is the right design correction?

options.A: Always retry on an empty result, since an empty list usually indicates a transient failure
options.B: Return `isError: true` for both cases so the agent never tells a customer they have no orders
options.C: Return a transient/retryable `isError` for the database failure and a normal empty result for no matches
options.D: Return a normal empty result for both and let the agent infer the difference from response latency

explanation: An access failure (database unreachable) and a valid empty result (query ran, zero matches) are different outcomes and need different signals. (C) makes the failure an `isError: true` with a transient/retryable category so the agent can retry or escalate, and leaves the genuine no-matches case as a successful empty result the agent can report truthfully.

distractors.A: Retrying every empty result burns calls on customers who genuinely have no orders, and still leaves the two cases indistinguishable.
distractors.B: Marking a valid empty result as an error means the agent can never truthfully answer the common case of a customer with no matching orders.
distractors.D: Latency is an unreliable proxy — a slow successful query looks like a failure — so the tool would be asking the agent to guess at something it can state outright.

stem: Your team needs Claude Code to query an internal, proprietary patient-records system in a HIPAA-regulated environment, with full audit logging and in-house control over data access. A popular community MCP server exists for a generic SQL database but not for this system. What is the appropriate choice?

options.A: Fork the community SQL server and ship it without reviewing its code, to save integration time
options.B: Build a custom MCP server for the proprietary records system, with audit logging and access controls
options.C: Use the community SQL MCP server, pointing it at the patient-records database to save build time
options.D: Skip MCP entirely and have developers paste the relevant patient records into the prompt by hand

explanation: Proprietary internal systems in regulated industries — custom business logic, audit requirements, in-house control over data access — are the canonical case for building a CUSTOM MCP server, which is (B). Community servers are the right call for standard integrations that match the common case, which a proprietary patient-records system does not.

distractors.A: Shipping unreviewed third-party code that touches protected health information is a security and compliance failure regardless of how much time it saves.
distractors.C: A generic SQL server cannot satisfy the proprietary schema, the audit trail, or the HIPAA access controls, and it points code you did not review at sensitive data.
distractors.D: Abandoning MCP forfeits structured, auditable tool access and makes the compliance problem worse: manual pasting is unlogged and error-prone.

stem: A single research agent has 17 tools and increasingly picks the wrong one, with slow, token-heavy selection turns. Following the tool-count heuristics, what is the most effective architectural change?

options.A: Merge the 17 into a handful of mega-tools that each take a `mode` parameter to select behavior
options.B: Partition the 17 tools across specialized subagents of 4-5 tools each, behind a coordinator
options.C: Add a few-shot example for each of the 17 tools so the model learns to select among them
options.D: Since the count is still under the 10-tool threshold, just rewrite the descriptions to be distinct

explanation: Once a tool set grows past roughly 15, the remedy is to PARTITION the tools across specialized subagents of about 4-5 tools each, with a coordinator delegating to them — option (B). Rewriting descriptions is the fix when the count is under about 10; at 17 tools, attention dilution and tool-space interference are the binding constraint and no amount of wording will remove them.

distractors.A: Mega-tools with a `mode` flag hide distinct capabilities behind one opaque parameter, so the selection problem moves from picking a tool to picking a mode.
distractors.C: Seventeen few-shot examples add substantial context on every turn while leaving the tool count — the actual cause of the degradation — untouched.
distractors.D: The premise is wrong: 17 is past the partition threshold, not under 10, so the description-rewrite remedy is being applied at the wrong scale.

stem: Three MCP tools each return data with different date formats: `get_customer` uses Unix timestamps, `lookup_order` uses ISO 8601, and `process_refund` returns numeric status codes. The agent occasionally misreads them. You cannot modify the upstream MCP servers. What is the best client-side fix?

options.A: Switch to a larger model whose stronger parsing handles the mixed date and status formats
options.B: Add a paragraph to the system prompt explaining how to interpret each tool's output format
options.C: Add few-shot examples demonstrating correct interpretation of each tool's output format
options.D: Use a PostToolUse hook to normalize each tool's output into one date and status format

explanation: A PostToolUse hook intercepts tool results and transforms them deterministically before the model ever processes them, which is exactly what normalizing Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 dates, and numeric status codes into a single representation requires — and it works without touching the upstream MCP servers, as the stem demands. (D) is the only deterministic option; (A), (B) and (C) all leave interpretation probabilistic.

distractors.A: A larger model costs more per call and still parses the mixed formats probabilistically, so misreads become rarer rather than impossible.
distractors.B: System-prompt instructions add token overhead on every turn and still depend on the model applying them correctly to each result.
distractors.C: Few-shot examples reduce the error rate without eliminating it, and consume context repeatedly for work a hook does once, exactly.

stem: Your `lookup_order` tool returns 42 fields per order, but the agent needs only 5 for return processing. Across long conversations the verbose results bloat context. You cannot change the MCP server, and the trimming logic is purely mechanical (keep a fixed field subset). What is the most appropriate mechanism?

options.A: A PostToolUse hook that trims each `lookup_order` result to the 5 needed fields
options.B: Raising `max_tokens` so the verbose 42-field results fit comfortably in the response
options.C: Asking customers to read their order details aloud so the tool call can be skipped
options.D: Instructions in CLAUDE.md telling the model to ignore the 37 fields it does not need

explanation: Trimming a known, fixed subset of fields is deterministic mechanical work — exactly what a PostToolUse hook is for. (A) strips the unused fields before the result enters context, preventing the bloat without modifying the MCP server the stem says you cannot change.

distractors.B: Raising `max_tokens` makes room for the waste instead of removing it; all 42 fields still accumulate across the conversation, worsening cost and dilution.
distractors.C: Pushing data entry onto the customer degrades the support experience and throws away the tool's value to avoid a problem the hook solves invisibly.
distractors.D: An instruction to ignore fields still loads all 42 into context on every call, so the context bloat the stem describes is unchanged.

stem: In your repo, Claude Code consistently reaches for the built-in Grep tool instead of your custom `search_internal_kb` MCP tool, even when the answer lives in the internal knowledge base. The MCP tool works when invoked manually. What is the best first remedy?

options.A: Lower the model temperature so it more consistently favors the MCP tool over the built-ins
options.B: Disable the built-in Grep tool for this repo so the model is forced to use the MCP tool
options.C: Move the MCP server configuration into CLAUDE.md so the model notices the tool exists
options.D: Enhance the `search_internal_kb` description to state what it returns and when to prefer it

explanation: When the model reaches for a built-in over an MCP tool that works fine when invoked directly, the usual cause is a description that does not make the tool's distinct capability and output obvious. (D) enhances what the model actually reads at selection time — what the tool does, what it returns, and when to prefer it over file-content search.

distractors.A: Temperature affects sampling randomness, not which tool semantically fits the request, so it cannot redirect selection toward the knowledge base.
distractors.B: Removing a working built-in to force a choice breaks legitimate file-content search across the repo, a heavy price for what is a wording problem.
distractors.C: MCP servers are configured in `.mcp.json` or `~/.claude.json`; describing one in CLAUDE.md does not register it and does not change tool selection.

stem: A reviewer argues: "We set `readOnlyHint: true` and `destructiveHint: false` on our `cancel_subscription` tool, so the host can safely auto-approve it without user confirmation." Why is this reasoning flawed?

options.A: Annotations apply only to resources, so they have no bearing on how tools get approved
options.B: The only flaw is the `readOnlyHint` value; set it to false and auto-approval becomes safe
options.C: The reasoning is sound; annotations are authoritative and hosts should trust them here
options.D: Annotations are untrusted hints; hosts must not base security decisions on them alone

explanation: Tool annotations are HINTS, not guarantees. The MCP spec states that clients and hosts MUST NOT make security-critical decisions based solely on annotations, because a server can advertise whatever values it likes — including `readOnlyHint: true` on a tool that cancels subscriptions. As (D) says, the host has to enforce its own authorization and confirmation policy regardless of what the tool claims about itself.

distractors.A: Annotations are a tool-definition feature (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, `openWorldHint`); the claim that they apply only to resources is simply false.
distractors.B: Correcting the value fixes the accuracy of the hint but not the reasoning: even accurate annotations are self-reported, so sole reliance on them stays unsafe.
distractors.C: Treating annotations as authoritative is precisely the delegation the spec warns against, since the server supplying them is the party being authorized.

stem: You want to guarantee that `validate_identity` runs before `process_refund` is ever callable, on every conversation, with no exceptions. A teammate proposes combining them into one tool; another proposes a forced `tool_choice`; another proposes a hook. Which gives the strongest, deterministic guarantee that verification is enforced?

options.A: Set `tool_choice: {type: tool, name: validate_identity}` on the first turn of the conversation
options.B: Add an emphatic system-prompt rule that the model must always verify identity before refunding
options.C: Implement a PreToolUse hook that blocks `process_refund` until `validate_identity` succeeds
options.D: Combine both into a single `validate_and_refund` tool so the two steps become inseparable

explanation: When a business rule needs a guarantee rather than a tendency, a hook is the enforcement point the model cannot route around: (C) blocks `process_refund` until `validate_identity` has succeeded in the session, whatever the model decides to do. Forced `tool_choice` and prompt rules are model-side and probabilistic, and merging the tools couples two concerns that should stay separable.

distractors.A: Forcing the first call only constrains turn one; nothing stops the model from calling `process_refund` later in the same conversation without re-verifying.
distractors.B: Prompt rules are followed most of the time, not all of the time, and the stem asks for a guarantee with no exceptions.
distractors.D: Merging removes the ability to verify identity independently and re-runs validation on every refund, including when identity was confirmed moments earlier.

stem: A subagent's `extract_fields` tool encounters three distinct failures while processing a batch: a rate-limit (HTTP 429) from the source API, a malformed input record, and an access-denied (403) on one protected document. To enable the best coordinator recovery, how should these be categorized?

options.A: Rate-limit and access-denied as `transient`/retryable, malformed input as `permission`
options.B: All three as `validation` errors, since each one involves bad or unacceptable input
options.C: All three as `transient` with `isRetryable: true`, since a uniform retry policy is simplest
options.D: Rate-limit as `transient`, malformed input as `validation`, access-denied as `permission`

explanation: Each failure maps to a distinct category with a distinct recovery: a 429 is `transient` and retryable (back off and retry), a malformed record is a `validation` error that is not retryable (it needs different input), and a 403 is a `permission` error that is not retryable (it needs different credentials). (D) is the only mapping that lets the coordinator retry exactly what is retryable and route the rest appropriately.

distractors.A: This swaps two categories: a 403 is a credential problem, not a transient one, and a malformed record is a data problem, not a permission one — so the coordinator retries the 403 forever and asks for new credentials for a bad record.
distractors.B: Calling a rate-limit and an access-denied `validation` errors hides the two recoveries that actually differ: one needs backoff, the other needs different credentials.
distractors.C: A uniform retry policy burns the batch's remaining budget re-sending a malformed record and a 403 document, neither of which can ever succeed on retry.

stem: Your repo has a project-scoped `github` MCP server in committed `.mcp.json`. A developer needs to temporarily point their own session at a forked, experimental GitHub MCP endpoint without changing the shared file or affecting teammates. Given the scope precedence (local > project > user), what should they do?

options.A: Add a user-scoped `github` server, since user scope overrides project scope globally
options.B: Add a local-scoped `github` entry pointing at the experimental fork's endpoint
options.C: Edit the committed `.mcp.json` to the experimental URL and revert it before pushing
options.D: Delete the project entry from `.mcp.json` so the experimental server is the only one

explanation: Local scope is private to one developer within one project and carries the highest precedence (local > project > user). Adding a local-scoped `github` entry, as in (B), shadows the shared project entry for that developer alone, leaving the committed `.mcp.json` and every teammate untouched.

distractors.A: User scope is the LOWEST precedence of the three, so the committed project entry would continue to win and the experimental endpoint would never be used.
distractors.C: Editing the shared file works only until someone forgets to revert, and it makes the developer's experiment one `git commit -a` away from everyone else's session.
distractors.D: Deleting the project entry is a change to the shared committed file, so it removes the `github` server for every teammate as soon as it is pushed.

stem: You gave the document-analysis agent a general-purpose `fetch_url` tool so it could download documents by URL. Production logs show this agent now frequently downloads search-engine results pages to perform ad hoc web search — behavior that should be routed through the web-search agent — causing inconsistent results. Which fix is most effective?

options.A: Replace `fetch_url` with a `load_document` tool that validates that URLs point to document formats
options.B: Remove `fetch_url` from the document-analysis agent and route all URL fetching through the coordinator to the web-search agent
options.C: Implement filtering that blocks `fetch_url` calls to known search-engine domains while allowing other URLs
options.D: Add instructions to the document-analysis agent's prompt that `fetch_url` should only be used to download document URLs, not to search

explanation: Replacing the general-purpose tool with a document-specific `load_document` tool that validates URL targets constrains capability at the interface level. This follows the principle of least privilege: the undesired search behavior becomes impossible rather than merely discouraged, while the agent keeps the document-download capability it legitimately needs.

distractors.B: Removing the tool entirely takes away a capability the agent legitimately needs (downloading documents by URL), forcing extra coordinator round trips for its core workflow.
distractors.C: A domain blocklist is brittle and incomplete — new or obscure search endpoints bypass it, so the misuse persists.
distractors.D: Prompt instructions are probabilistic; the over-broad capability remains available, so misuse is discouraged but not prevented.

stem: Production logs show a consistent pattern: when customers include the word "account" in their message (e.g., "I want to check my account for an order I made yesterday"), the agent calls `get_customer` first 78% of the time; when customers phrase similar requests without "account" (e.g., "I want to check an order I made yesterday"), it calls `lookup_order` first 93% of the time. Tool descriptions are clear and unambiguous. What is the most likely root cause of this discrepancy?

options.A: The system prompt contains keyword-sensitive routing instructions that steer selection on terms like "account."
options.B: The model's base training associates "account" terminology with customer operations, overriding the descriptions.
options.C: The model needs fine-tuning on multi-concept messages that contain both account and order terminology.
options.D: The tool descriptions need negative examples specifying when NOT to use each tool, to stop the confusion.

explanation: A split this sharp and this systematic — 78% versus 93%, conditioned on the presence of a single word — points to explicit routing logic somewhere in the prompt reacting to "account" and steering the agent toward customer-related tools. Since the stem states the tool descriptions are clear and unambiguous, the prompt's own instructions are the remaining source of the steering, which is what (A) identifies.

distractors.B: Base-training associations produce diffuse tendencies across many phrasings, not a clean split conditioned on one keyword; a pattern this systematic indicates explicit instructions.
distractors.C: Fine-tuning is not how tool selection is steered in this architecture, and a 78/93 split on one word is far too clean to be a training-data coverage gap.
distractors.D: This treats the symptom at the wrong layer — the stem rules out description ambiguity, so rewriting descriptions cannot remove steering that originates in the prompt.

stem: Your `remove_team_member` tool uses a `dry_run: boolean` parameter so impacts can be previewed before execution, but production monitoring shows the agent bypasses the preview step by calling with `dry_run=false` directly. You need to guarantee that every removal is preceded by a preview that the user explicitly confirms. What is the most reliable approach?

options.A: Add server-side validation permitting `dry_run=false` only if an identical `dry_run=true` call ran in the last 60 seconds.
options.B: Annotate the tool as requiring confirmation and have the orchestration layer prompt for approval before forwarding calls.
options.C: Add instructions and few-shot examples to the tool description requiring a `dry_run=true` call and confirmation first.
options.D: Split it into `preview_remove_member`, returning impacts plus a single-use token, and `execute_remove_member`, which requires it.

explanation: The two-tool token-binding design in (D) makes executing a removal without a prior preview architecturally impossible: `execute_remove_member` will not run without a single-use confirmation token, and only `preview_remove_member` can mint one. The constraint lives in code at the tool boundary, so it does not depend on LLM compliance, on timing heuristics, or on a host you may not control.

distractors.A: A 60-second window is a heuristic in both directions — the agent can fire a preview and execute a millisecond later with no human in the loop, and a user who deliberates for two minutes is locked out.
distractors.B: Annotations are advisory hints that hosts are free to ignore, so this moves the guarantee out of your tool and into infrastructure you do not control.
distractors.C: Description-level instructions depend on exactly the LLM compliance that production monitoring already shows is failing.

stem: Production monitoring shows your `search_catalog` tool fails 12% of the time: 8% are network timeouts that succeed when retried, and 4% are query syntax errors that never succeed regardless of retries. Both error types are currently returned identically, causing the agent to waste retries on unfixable errors. How should you modify the tool's error handling?

options.A: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing how to distinguish network errors from syntax errors.
options.B: Apply uniform exponential-backoff retry logic to every error the tool returns, up to a fixed attempt cap.
options.C: Retry network timeouts with backoff inside the tool, and return syntax errors immediately with validation details.
options.D: Return every error with a `retryable` boolean and error-type details, and let the agent decide whether to retry.

explanation: Retrying a transient failure is deterministic plumbing the tool can do itself, because the tool has definitive knowledge of which error it just hit. (C) handles the 8% of timeouts internally and returns the 4% of syntax errors immediately with parameter-validation details the agent can act on — mechanical retries in code, semantic correction with the model, each at the right abstraction boundary.

distractors.A: Few-shot examples ask the model to classify probabilistically what the tool already knows deterministically, placing the logic at the wrong layer.
distractors.B: Uniform backoff spends latency and cost retrying the 4% of syntax errors that can never succeed, which is the exact waste the stem asks you to eliminate.
distractors.D: A `retryable` flag beats undifferentiated errors, but it still delegates mechanical retry behavior to an agent that may not follow it consistently on every call.

stem: A research subagent wraps a flaky external API in a custom MCP tool. When the API returns HTTP 503, the tool handler raises an unhandled exception, which the MCP server turns into a JSON-RPC error response. The coordinating agent never adapts — it just reports "the tool failed" and stops. What is the correct way to surface a recoverable API failure so the model can act on it?

options.A: Increase the subagent's `max_tokens` so it has room to describe the failure in full
options.B: Catch the exception and return a normal result with `isError: true` describing the 503 and a retry
options.C: Let it propagate as a JSON-RPC error with a lower code so the model treats it as recoverable
options.D: Log the exception server-side and return an empty successful result so the agent continues

explanation: An uncaught exception becomes a protocol-level JSON-RPC error, which the model never sees — so the coordinating agent has nothing to reason about and simply stops. A recoverable execution failure should be caught in the handler and returned as a normal tool result with `isError: true` plus a descriptive, actionable message naming the 503 and suggesting a retry, as in (B), so the model can back off or try an alternative.

distractors.A: `max_tokens` governs output length, not error visibility; the model still never sees a protocol-layer error no matter how much room it has to write.
distractors.C: Everything in the JSON-RPC `error` field is hidden from the model regardless of its numeric code, so tuning the code changes nothing the agent can act on.
distractors.D: Returning an empty success suppresses the failure entirely, so the agent proceeds as though the fetch worked and reports results built on missing data.

stem: You are designing the structured error payload your `process_return` tool returns alongside `isError: true`. Beyond a human-readable message, which TWO additions most improve the agent's ability to recover appropriately? Select TWO.

options.A: A machine-readable `errorCategory` the agent can branch on, such as `transient` or `permission`
options.B: The full server stack trace, including internal file paths and line numbers, for debugging
options.C: An `isRetryable` boolean stating whether retrying the identical call could ever succeed
options.D: A monotonically increasing request sequence number attached to every call the tool receives

explanation: A machine-readable category (`transient`, `validation`, `permission`, `business`) lets the agent branch its recovery — retry, seek an alternative, or escalate — and an `isRetryable` flag answers directly whether the same call is worth repeating. (A) and (C) together with the human-readable message turn an opaque failure into an actionable one.

distractors.B: A raw stack trace leaks internal paths, fills context with frames the model cannot act on, and still does not say whether a retry would help.
distractors.D: Sequence numbers are server-side bookkeeping; knowing a call was the 47th informs no recovery decision the agent has to make.

stem: A subagent calls a `fetch_paper` tool that returns `isError: true`, `errorCategory: "transient"`, `isRetryable: true` for a rate-limited source. The subagent retries with backoff, but after several attempts the source is still rate-limited and the task deadline is approaching. According to sound multi-agent error handling, what should the subagent do next?

options.A: Keep retrying indefinitely, since a transient/retryable error means the call will eventually succeed
options.B: Silently return the partial results it already has as a normal success, without mentioning the failure
options.C: Stop local retries and propagate a structured error, with any partial results, for the coordinator to act on
options.D: Escalate to a human operator immediately on the first retryable error, before any local recovery

explanation: The pattern is bounded local recovery followed by propagation: handle transient failures locally, and when they do not clear, pass the failure upward with enough structured context — what failed, what was tried, any partial results, suggested alternatives — for the coordinator to decide between an alternate source, partial data, or escalation. (C) is that pattern; the deadline in the stem is what makes further local retries the wrong call.

distractors.A: "Retryable" means a retry is worth attempting, not that success is guaranteed; unbounded retries blow the deadline the stem sets and burn budget the coordinator could spend elsewhere.
distractors.B: Presenting partial results as a clean success hides the gap, so the coordinator cannot judge whether the data is complete enough to build on.
distractors.D: Escalating on the first retryable error skips the cheap bounded retry that resolves most rate limits, and the stem says several attempts had already been made.

stem: In MCP's two-layer error model, some failures belong in the JSON-RPC `error` field (protocol layer, hidden from the model) and others belong in the tool `result` with `isError: true` (execution layer, visible to the model). Which TWO of the following should be returned as tool-execution errors the model can see and act on? Select TWO.

options.A: The upstream payments API returns HTTP 429 (rate limited) while the tool is executing
options.B: The client calls a tool name the server does not expose, because of a typo in the name
options.C: The requested refund exceeds the agent's policy limit and must be routed to a manager
options.D: The client sends arguments that violate the tool's `inputSchema` (a required field is missing)

explanation: A runtime rate-limit (A) and a business-rule violation (C) are execution-time outcomes of a valid call: the model should see them and reason about backing off or routing to manager approval, so they belong in the `result` with `isError: true`. An unknown tool name and schema-invalid arguments are protocol-layer faults the server rejects before execution, so they go in the JSON-RPC `error` field the model does not see.

distractors.B: An unknown tool name is rejected at the protocol layer before any handler runs, so there is no execution result to mark and nothing for the model to recover from.
distractors.D: Arguments failing `inputSchema` validation are an invalid-params protocol error; the call never executes, so it cannot produce an execution-time result.

stem: Your data MCP server lets the agent query a large analytics warehouse. Today the agent burns several tool calls at the start of each task just to discover table and column names before it can write a correct query. Following the MCP control model, what is the cleanest way to give the agent this visibility?

options.A: Expose the schema (tables, columns, types) as an MCP resource and keep querying as a tool
options.B: Add `list_tables` and `describe_table` tools so the agent can explore the schema by calling them
options.C: Expose the schema as a tool and the query capability as a read-only resource the agent reads
options.D: Paste the full warehouse schema into the system prompt on every request the agent handles

explanation: Schema is read-only reference data the model reasons FROM, which is precisely what MCP resources are for (application-controlled data), while running a query is a model-controlled action that stays a tool. (A) gives the agent up-front visibility of tables and columns and removes the exploratory tool calls the stem is complaining about.

distractors.B: Discovery tools do work, but they reintroduce the very exploratory round trips you are trying to eliminate — the agent still spends calls learning what it could have been handed.
distractors.C: This inverts the control model: static schema is not an action the model chooses to take, and executing a query is not read-only reference data.
distractors.D: Hardcoding the whole schema into every prompt pays the full token cost on every turn regardless of need, and the copy goes stale as the warehouse changes.

stem: From your MCP server, a teammate exposes a reusable "open-a-bug-triage" workflow that a developer can invoke by name to pre-fill a structured, parameterized message (severity, component, repro steps) that kicks off a consistent triage conversation. In MCP terms, which primitive is this, and how does it differ from a tool?

options.A: A resource — because it supplies read-only reference data that the model reasons from
options.B: A tool — because the model autonomously decides to call it during its own reasoning
options.C: A prompt — a user-initiated, parameterized template, not a model-invoked action
options.D: An annotation — metadata hints attached to a tool definition to describe its behavior

explanation: An MCP prompt is a reusable, parameterized message template that a user deliberately invokes — often surfaced as a slash command — to standardize a workflow or kick off a task consistently, which is exactly the bug-triage workflow described. (C) contrasts it correctly with a tool, which the model chooses to call on its own to take an action, and with a resource, which is read-only data the model reasons from.

distractors.A: A resource is data the model reads for context, not an invokable template that takes parameters like severity and repro steps and starts a conversation.
distractors.B: A tool is invoked autonomously by the model to perform an action; this workflow is triggered by a developer and shapes the request itself rather than acting on the world.
distractors.D: Annotations are hint metadata attached to a tool definition (`readOnlyHint` and friends), not a standalone primitive anyone can invoke by name.

stem: You are deploying a central "CRM lookup" MCP server that dozens of support agents on different machines must reach over the network, with multiple concurrent connections. Which transport is the appropriate choice for this server?

options.A: stdio, running the server as a subprocess on each support agent's own machine
options.B: Streamable HTTP, exposing a single network endpoint that supports POST and GET
options.C: Legacy HTTP+SSE, the recommended default for new multi-user networked servers
options.D: No transport is needed; multi-user servers talk over the JSON-RPC error channel

explanation: Streamable HTTP is the current standard for remote, networked, multi-user MCP servers — a single endpoint handling POST and GET, which is what (B) describes and what dozens of agents on different machines need. stdio is for local integrations where the server runs as a subprocess of one host, and legacy SSE is deprecated.

distractors.A: stdio gives every machine its own subprocess, so there is no shared, network-reachable service and no way to hold multiple concurrent connections to one server.
distractors.C: HTTP+SSE was deprecated in favor of Streamable HTTP, so calling it the recommended default for new servers inverts the current guidance.
distractors.D: There is no transport-free mode and no "error channel" to communicate over; the JSON-RPC `error` field carries failures, not traffic.

stem: Your `extract_invoice` tool takes a single free-text `format` string parameter, and the model frequently passes unsupported or misspelled values ("pdf/a", "PDF-A", "Acrobat"), which the tool then rejects. The tool only ever supports three formats. What is the most reliable fix?

options.A: Add a paragraph to the system prompt listing the three valid format strings the model may use
options.B: Add a few-shot example for each of the three formats so the model learns the accepted spellings
options.C: Post-process the argument server-side, guessing the intended format by fuzzy string matching
options.D: Constrain the parameter in the tool's `inputSchema` to an `enum` of the three supported values

explanation: The `inputSchema` is the deterministic contract for a tool's arguments. Encoding the three allowed values as an `enum` — with a clear field description — both guides the model toward valid inputs and rejects invalid ones structurally at the interface, which is what (D) does. Prompt text and few-shot examples are probabilistic and leave the free-text parameter open, and fuzzy server-side guessing invites silent misclassification.

distractors.A: System-prompt instructions are probabilistic and the parameter still accepts any string, so "Acrobat" remains a value the model can pass.
distractors.B: Examples reduce bad inputs without eliminating them and cost tokens every turn, when the schema can encode the same constraint once and enforce it.
distractors.C: Fuzzy matching can silently resolve "pdf/a" to the wrong format, converting a loud rejection into a quiet extraction error nobody notices.

stem: Every response from your extraction pipeline must be a structured record produced by your single `emit_record` tool — free-text answers are never acceptable, and that is the only tool available. Which configuration most directly guarantees the model returns its output through that tool on each call?

options.A: Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "tool", "name": "emit_record"}` so the model must call it
options.B: Leave `tool_choice` on `auto` and add a strong system-prompt rule to always call `emit_record`
options.C: Lower the temperature to 0 so the model deterministically chooses to call `emit_record`
options.D: Remove the tool and ask the model to return JSON in plain text, validating the output afterward

explanation: Forcing tool use through `tool_choice` — `{"type":"tool","name":"emit_record"}`, or equivalently `{"type":"any"}` when that is the only tool available — is the direct, deterministic way to require that the model's output arrives through a specific tool, which is what (A) sets up. Prompt instructions and temperature are probabilistic and can still yield a free-text answer.

distractors.B: An `auto` tool_choice plus a prompt rule leaves the free-text path open, so some fraction of calls still return prose the pipeline cannot ingest.
distractors.C: Temperature affects sampling randomness, not whether the model calls a tool; a deterministic sample of a free-text answer is still a free-text answer.
distractors.D: Dropping the tool abandons the structured-output guarantee entirely and moves validation after the fact, which is the failure mode the stem rules out.

stem: Your `issue_gift_card` tool sometimes gets called twice for the same customer when a network hiccup causes the agent to retry, producing duplicate gift cards. You want retries to be safe without duplicating side effects. What is the most robust tool-design fix?

options.A: Accept an `idempotency_key`; a repeat call with the same key returns the original result
options.B: Add a note to the tool description telling the model never to retry `issue_gift_card`
options.C: Set `idempotentHint: true` in the annotations so hosts know the operation is safe to repeat
options.D: Wrap the tool in a PreToolUse hook that blocks a second call within five seconds of the first

explanation: True idempotency comes from a client-supplied key the tool persists: (A) records the key, performs the side effect at most once, and returns the original result on any repeat, so a retry after a network hiccup is genuinely safe. An annotation only advertises idempotency, a description note relies on model compliance, and a fixed time window is a heuristic.

distractors.B: A description note asks the model not to retry, which neither prevents the client from retrying nor stops a duplicate card when a retry does happen.
distractors.C: `idempotentHint: true` claims the property without implementing it; the second call still issues a second gift card, and now the host has been told it is safe.
distractors.D: A five-second window misses retries that arrive later and wrongly blocks two legitimately distinct gift-card requests for the same customer.

stem: A research subagent only needs to run read-only SELECT queries against a reporting database, but it is given a general `run_sql` tool that can execute any statement, including INSERT, UPDATE, and DROP. What change best applies the principle of least privilege?

options.A: Keep `run_sql` but add a system-prompt rule that the agent may only write SELECT statements
options.B: Expose a narrower read-only query tool, or back `run_sql` with a read-only database role
options.C: Keep `run_sql` but set `readOnlyHint: true` so the host knows the tool is safe to call
options.D: Keep `run_sql` and rely on code review to catch dangerous statements the agent generates

explanation: Least privilege means the undesired capability is impossible at the interface, not merely discouraged. (B) removes write and DDL power structurally — either by exposing a purpose-built read-only query tool or by backing `run_sql` with a read-only database role — so a mistaken or prompt-injected agent cannot drop a table. Prompt rules and annotations are advisory and leave the capability in place.

distractors.A: A prompt rule is probabilistic and leaves full write and DDL capability available, so one bad generation or a single prompt injection can still destroy data.
distractors.C: `readOnlyHint: true` is a non-authoritative hint about the tool, not a constraint on what it can execute; the write capability is entirely untouched.
distractors.D: Code review happens before or after the fact, not at the moment the agent issues a statement, so it cannot stop a destructive query at runtime.

stem: Your `search_knowledge_base` tool currently returns the full text of every matching article inline — often 40+ long articles — and across a multi-turn conversation this floods the context window and degrades the agent. The agent usually needs only one or two articles in full. What is the best tool-design change?

options.A: Return a ranked list of summaries (title, id, snippet) plus a `get_article` tool for full text
options.B: Raise the conversation's context limit so all 40 full articles fit without being truncated
options.C: Keep returning everything but instruct the agent in CLAUDE.md to ignore the articles it does not need
options.D: Return all 40 full articles but compress them by stripping whitespace and punctuation

explanation: The design fix is to return a small, ranked set of concise summaries and let the agent pull full text on demand for the one or two articles it actually needs, as in (A) — large payloads stay out of context until they are required. Raising limits or stripping whitespace merely accommodates the bloat, and a CLAUDE.md instruction still loads all 40 articles every turn.

distractors.B: A bigger window makes room for the waste rather than removing it, and cost and attention dilution keep growing as the conversation goes on.
distractors.C: Telling the agent to ignore unused articles still places all 40 full texts in context on every turn, so the flooding and the degradation persist.
distractors.D: Stripping whitespace shaves a small percentage off dozens of full articles; the volume, not the formatting, is what floods the window.
